title: Dalton Caldwell on pivoting: when, why and how to change your startup idea
summary: Dalton Caldwell explains that pivoting is just changing your idea and should feel lightweight early on. He covers why founders pivot too late (loss aversion, politeness mistaken for traction), good and bad reasons to pivot, and a four-part scoring rubric for the next idea, illustrated with YC examples like Brex, Retool, Magic and Segment.

principles.text: Pivoting is just changing your idea; early on it should feel lightweight and happen constantly.
principles.quote: if you're not in a state where you're rapidly changing ideas or assumptions over and over and over again in quick succession, you are likely doing it wrong. You are likely moving too slow.

principles.text: Pivot because of opportunity cost: months of full-time effort without results is the strongest signal.
principles.quote: by working on something that's not working and you have evidence that it's not working, you are taking opportunity cost to not be doing something else.

principles.text: Don't confuse customer politeness with traction; polite feedback can keep you looping for years.
principles.quote: a lot of founders get confused about politeness and getting that confused with traction.

principles.text: A little traction is a trap; a total failure lets you move on immediately with no regrets.
principles.quote: I call it the uncanny valley of product market fit.

principles.text: Take several high-quality shots on goal; each full build-ship-learn iteration is another roll of the dice at product market fit.
principles.quote: it's much easier to be lucky when you get like half a dozen shots on goal than one

principles.text: Score a new idea on size, founder-market fit, ease of getting started, and early market feedback; easy-to-start ideas are undersold.
principles.quote: getting find an idea that's easy to get started with um is just as important as the idea itself.
